extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating a beat sheet to outline the key events/beats of a film or TV episode so the narrative is structured, paced, and suitable for pitching or collaboration. Applies to short and feature runtimes (e.g., 30/60/90 minutes) and multiple screenwriting methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: beat sheet outlines key events
rubrics_metrics.description: A beat sheet is a tool used in screenwriting to outline the key events or ‘beats’ in a story. It serves as a guide for structuring the narrative and helps writers ensure important plot points and moments of character development are included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a beat sheet to list critical moments so you can see the flow of the story and place plot twists and character development in the right place for maximum impact. Can be written for an episode or a film.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beats must move the story forward
rubrics_metrics.description: In a script, a beat refers to a specific moment or action in a scene that moves the story forward (e.g., a character's big decision, a change in direction of a conversation, or a joke landing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing beats, ensure each one is something significant that advances plot, character, or conflict; avoid beats that are merely filler or do not affect the narrative trajectory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale the beat sheet to runtime
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a beat sheet appropriate to the length of the project — for a 30‑minute episode, a 60‑minute episode, a 90‑minute film, etc., outlining all key points that need coverage within that runtime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the number and granularity of beats match the available screen time so pacing and development feel natural; don’t cram too many beats into too short a runtime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a structural framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Beat sheets act as a structural framework: listing key plot points makes writing scenes easier because you know exactly what to include and how things should flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the beat sheet as the story's skeleton to guide scene construction and to keep narrative cohesion during drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use beat sheets for story planning and to identify gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing out all the beats enables you to clearly see gaps and inconsistencies in your plot and to identify characters or storylines that need further development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review the sheet to spot missing motivations, underdeveloped arcs, or inconsistencies before writing full scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refinement: assess whether each beat contributes
rubrics_metrics.description: A beat sheet is a revision tool: writers should review beats and assess whether each contributes effectively to the overall narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a beat or subplot isn’t pulling its weight, remove it or rework it. Use the sheet to refine and improve story economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing and rhythm through beat placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Breaking the story into beats allows strategic placement of tension, humour, revelation, or excitement to build momentum and drive the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan where to escalate stakes, insert comic beats, or breathe between big moments to achieve desired rhythm across the runtime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat sheet as reference for original ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: As projects change over time, a beat sheet serves as a raw source of inspiration and a reference to return to original story elements if they get diluted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep and consult the beat sheet during rewrites to maintain the project’s core intentions and themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise communication for pitching
rubrics_metrics.description: A beat sheet shows that a writer has a clear vision for the project and provides a concise and efficient way to communicate the essence of the story to potential investors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When pitching, present the beat sheet to communicate the narrative quickly and clearly — time-limited settings benefit from a tight, readable sheet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaboration: clear overview for production partners
rubrics_metrics.description: Beat sheets are useful when working with others (directors, producers), giving everyone a concise overview of a story’s structure and key beats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the beat sheet as a shared reference to keep collaborators aligned on story beats, tone, and pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-act structure beat sheet
rubrics_metrics.description: A traditional beat sheet aligned with the three-act structure: outlines key beats for each act, including the introduction, rising action, climax, falling action, and resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map major plot milestones to act breaks (beginning/midpoint/end) to ensure broader structural integrity and act-level pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Save the Cat beat sheet (15 beats)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Save the Cat method (Blake Snyder) outlines 15 key beats spread across the story, including elements like the opening image, catalyst, midpoint, and the 'save the cat' moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this popular, prescriptive beat list if you want a specific, industry-recognised template — it emphasizes likability, turning points, and beat spacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero's Journey beat sheet (17 steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hero’s Journey is a 17-step story structure describing how a hero leaves the known world, faces trials and transformation, and returns changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this mythic arc when your story benefits from an explicitly transformational protagonist journey with ritualised stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mini movie beat sheet
rubrics_metrics.description: A mini movie beat sheet divides the script into ‘mini movies’ within acts, each with its own set of beats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this approach to keep momentum by treating sections of the script as smaller, complete dramatic arcs — helpful for episodic TV or multi-thread narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening image
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce the audience to the story’s world: a short description of the very first moment, event, or people viewers will see.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an image that sets tone, theme, or contrasts with the final image to highlight change across the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce your main character: their motivations, what they want, and what’s preventing them from getting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly establish protagonist goals, flaws, and the status quo so subsequent beats have stakes and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of theme
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell the audience what your film, sitcom or drama is about — the thematic statement or question the story explores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weave theme into early beats so later events resonate; theme can be explicit or implicit but should be trackable across beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inciting incident
rubrics_metrics.description: The event that should propel the protagonist into action, initiating the central conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place this early enough to justify the protagonist’s journey and clearly change the protagonist’s circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debate
rubrics_metrics.description: After the inciting incident, a period where the character experiences inner turmoil, debate, argument, or reflection about a significant decision or conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this beat to show stakes and resistance; it helps motivate the protagonist’s next move and deepen character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subplot
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary storylines (e.g., a love story) that run alongside the main plot; include these so they can be properly woven into the narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline subplots in the beat sheet and plan their intersections with main beats to support theme and character development without cluttering the main arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second turning point
rubrics_metrics.description: The moment that intensifies the central conflict and pushes the story toward the climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this beat to raise stakes and force decisive action leading into the climax; it should feel like an escalation rather than a repeat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climax
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the highest point of tension where the main conflict reaches its peak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the climax the most consequential confrontation or decision, resolving the central dramatic question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline (aftermath/resolution beats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beats that address the aftermath of the climax, resolving subplots and character arcs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan how consequences of the climax play out and tidy up loose ends; ensure resolutions feel earned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finale
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclude with final beats that provide closure to the main storylines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver emotional and thematic closure; echo or contrast the opening image where appropriate to underline change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional/additional beats to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Other beats you might include: character introductions, foreshadowing for future events, red herrings, and the 'all is lost' moment where the protagonist faces their lowest point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor additional beats to genre and tone. The 'all is lost' beat often precedes the second turning point/climax and is useful for dramatic stakes.
